--- Page 1 ---
SPECEVO: SPECULATIVE EVOLUTION WITH LARGE
LANGUAGE MODELS FOR COST-EFFICIENT SCIENTIFIC
DISCOVERY
Ha Minh Hieu1,*
Tongyao Zhu2,†
Do Xuan Long2,†
Min-Yen Kan2,†
1Hanoi University of Science and Technology, 2National University of Singapore
haminhhieu1005@gmail.com
{tongyao.zhu,xuanlong.do}@u.nus.edu
knmnyn@nus.edu.sg
ABSTRACT
LLM-driven evolutionary search is a promising paradigm for scientific discovery,
but existing methods remain costly and slow, often applying expensive reasoning
uniformly while underusing evidence from failed, redundant, and saturated trials.
We introduce Speculative Evolution (SPECEVO), a multi-LLM framework that
coordinates lightweight and frontier models through continual consolidation of
search evidence. Lightweight models power both parallel Speculators, which gen-
erate and refine candidate programs, and an Advisor, which distills accumulated
successes, failures, and saturated directions into persistent guidance for subse-
quent exploration. At sparse checkpoints, a frontier-model Navigator inspects the
evolving population and intervenes through synthesis, surgical refinement, or re-
framing according to search stagnation. This speculate-then-consolidate workflow
delegates routine exploration and evidence consolidation to inexpensive models
while reserving frontier reasoning for strategic interventions whose benefits extend
across many subsequent low-cost evaluations. Across 176 tasks spanning four
scientific and algorithmic discovery domains, SPECEVO matches or outperforms
frontier-model baselines while reducing API cost by up to 80%, achieves up to
1.5× greater evaluation efficiency than cost-efficient baselines on equation discov-
ery, and improves over the strongest CO-Bench baseline by 3.8%. These results
support trajectory-conditioned model coordination as an effective approach to
cost-efficient scientific discovery. 3
1
INTRODUCTION
Recent advances in large language models have enabled a new paradigm of evolutionary search
for automated scientific discovery (Yamada et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b). LLMs act as semantic
variation operators, proposing meaningful modifications to candidate programs that are refined
through execution-based evaluation and selection (Liu et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2024). Such approaches
have achieved strong results across mathematical discovery, combinatorial optimization, and systems
engineering (Hieu et al., 2026; Cemri et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b).
Despite their strong results, many systems nevertheless use a single backbone for candidate generation
and higher-level search decisions (Agrawal et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b).
When that backbone is a frontier model, routine proposals repeatedly incur expensive inference.
Figure 1 illustrates the resulting performance–cost trade-off: using lightweight backbones lowers
API expenditure but can substantially reduce solution quality in the evaluated baselines. Lightweight
models offer inexpensive exploration, but without reusable guidance they can repeatedly revisit similar
strategies or reproduce implementation errors (Dat et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024a). Merely generating
more affordable proposals therefore does not ensure sustained search progress. Heterogeneous-model
approaches address part of this problem by assigning different search operations to different models
*Work done during the internship at WING, NUS.

3Our code is available at https://github.com/langkhachhoha/SpecEvo

or transferring a population from lightweight exploration to frontier-model refinement (Tanveer, 2026;
Luo et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026). These approaches motivate a complementary question: How
can accumulated successes, failures, and signs of saturation continually inform both subsequent
lightweight proposals and the scope of frontier-model intervention?

Figure 1: Top: Performance vs. API cost on mathe-
matical discovery tasks; SPECEVO forms the Pareto
frontier. Bottom: Best-so-far NMSE on LSR-Synth
Biology and Chemistry over 500 evaluations.
To address these gaps, we present SPECEVO,
a multi-LLM evolutionary framework orga-
nized around a workflow we call speculate-
then-consolidate (StC). StC repeatedly con-
verts accumulated search evidence into guid-
ance and strategic interventions that inform
subsequent low-cost exploration; SPECEVO
provides its concrete realization through
specialized model roles and shared search
state.
Consolidation occurs periodically
while lightweight exploration continues. A
central design choice is to distinguish the
programs retained for further search from the
evidence retained for learning. An adaptive
MAP-Elites-style (Mouret & Clune, 2015)
archive maintains one elite per structural–
semantic niche, allowing programs outside
the global top ranks to remain available when
they improve their own niches. A separate
history records all evaluated attempts, in-
cluding rejected programs and execution fail-
ures. Together, these structures expose which
strategies remain competitive, which direc-
tions consume evaluations without progress,
and which implementation errors recur.
This evidence supports both revisable guidance for
lightweight models and search-state-dependent choices about frontier intervention. Across model
configurations, SPECEVO improves the performance–cost trade-off over methods built around a
single frontier model. Its advantages over cost-efficient allocation strategies persist under matched
model-call and evaluation budgets, supporting the value of coordinating model use through accumu-
lated search evidence. Ablations and search-trajectory analyses further support the importance of
preserving diverse candidates, adapting intervention scope to stagnation, and revising guidance as
evidence accumulates. Our main contributions are:
• We introduce SPECEVO, an asynchronous realization of StC with parallel lightweight
Speculators, a lightweight Advisor, and a sparsely invoked frontier-model Navigator.
• We develop coordinated feedback mechanisms that combine failure- and niche-progress-
aware guidance with a stagnation signal controlling parent sampling and selecting among
synthesis, surgical refinement, and reframing at fixed Navigator checkpoints.
• We provide a systematic evaluation on 176 tasks spanning mathematical discovery, systems
optimization, combinatorial optimization, and scientific equation discovery, combining
comparisons under matched budgets with controlled model-allocation studies, component
ablations, and analyses of search dynamics.
2
RELATED WORK
LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search. FunSearch and AlphaEvolve demonstrate how execution-based
selection can turn LLM-generated program variations into mathematical and systems discoveries
(Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). Subsequent work addresses two complementary
challenges within this loop. The first is preserving useful alternatives: OpenEvolve combines island
evolution with quality-diversity archiving, while SeaEvo organizes search around persistent strategy-
level memory (Sharma, 2025; Luo et al., 2026b). These designs retain alternatives that can support
exploration beyond the current best program. The second is using evaluation feedback to improve
search decisions: GEPA derives reflective updates and maintains complementary candidates through
2


--- Page 3 ---
Pareto selection, AdaEvolve adapts exploration and resource allocation to observed progress, and
EvoX evolves the search policy itself (Agrawal et al., 2025; Cemri et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b).
SPECEVO builds on these principles, using archive- and trajectory-level evidence to coordinate
lightweight exploration, guidance revision, and frontier intervention.
Cost-Efficient LLM Allocation. Cost-efficient LLM systems commonly coordinate cheap and strong
models through cascades or adaptive routing (Chen et al., 2023b; Aggarwal et al., 2024; Ding et al.,
2024; Ong et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). SCOPE uses query-level partial evaluations to select a
fixed model assignment for each module of a compound system under a quality constraint (Huang
et al., 2026). While reducing configuration-search cost, it does not adapt allocation to an evolving
search state. Within evolutionary search, LEVI combines diversity preservation and proxy evaluation
with role-aware routing, assigning local refinements to cheap models and paradigm shifts to a frontier
model (Tanveer, 2026). However, the frontier model remains tied to a predefined role, while its
error-oriented advice does not use broader progress and saturation evidence to adapt interventions.
RelayEvolve develops multiple cheap-model trajectories and performs a one-time handoff of a
quality-diverse population to strong-model refinement (Luo et al., 2026a). Afterward, lightweight
exploration ends, and evidence from discarded or exhausted trajectories is not consolidated into
reusable guidance. SPECEVO instead continually consolidates accumulated evidence to guide both
lightweight exploration and state-dependent frontier-model intervention.
3
METHODOLOGY
Figure 2 summarizes how SPECEVO initializes its population and coordinates the subsequent search,
while Appendices D and H provide the complete algorithms and prompt templates, respectively.
3.1
MOTIVATION: FROM SPECULATIVE DECODING TO SPECULATIVE EVOLUTION
Speculative decoding uses lightweight drafts and parallel verification by a stronger model to amortize
inference while preserving the target distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a). Related
evolutionary methods likewise reserve stronger models for difficult mutations or structural changes
(Ray et al., 2026; Tanveer, 2026). In SPECEVO, candidate quality is established by an executable
evaluator, while accumulated outcomes inform future proposals. The speculate-then-consolidate
(StC) workflow therefore transfers the principle of asymmetric computation to search trajectories:
inexpensive exploration supplies evidence, and periodic consolidation turns that evidence into
guidance and strategic proposals for subsequent exploration.
Figure 2 separates population initialization on the left from the ongoing StC loop on the right. Initial-
ization proceeds from seed generation through lightweight diversification to population embedding.
The resulting archive supports continuous Speculator exploration, while the Navigator above and
the Advisor below provide strategic proposals and reusable guidance at slower cadences. Once the
prescribed budget is exhausted, the search terminates and the highest-scoring program in the final
archive is returned. We next describe the shared search state and each functional role.
Problem setup.
Given a task T with a space P of executable candidate programs and an evaluator
F : P →R, we aim to discover p⋆= arg maxp∈P F(p) under a prescribed wall-clock, API-cost, or
evaluation budget. At evaluation step t, we maintain two shared structures: a behavioral archive At
retaining a bounded set of competitive programs, and a search history Ht recording every evaluated
attempt, including rejected candidates and execution failures. Each stored program p is paired with a
natural-language description d(p) of its strategy, supplied by the generating model.
Initialization.
The Generate seed programs block in Figure 2 provides diverse, verified starting
hypotheses. The Navigator uses the frontier model MN to generate M=5 seed programs sequentially,
conditioning each call on the strategies and evaluation outcomes of earlier seeds. The prompt asks
the model to identify their algorithmic paradigms and propose a different modeling, decomposition,
construction, or search strategy. In the subsequent Generate variants block, the Speculator pool
uses the lightweight model MS to expand each executable seed into V =20 inexpensive variants in
parallel, drawing on ninsp ∈{1, 2} other seeds as inspiration. We initialize the behavioral archive
from these evaluated programs using the representation and admission rule described next.
3


--- Page 4 ---
Behavioral archive.
Fitness alone does not distinguish the strategies implemented by candidate
programs. A population selected solely by global fitness can become dominated by variants of
one strategy, discarding lower-scoring alternatives that may provide complementary mechanisms or
promising starting points for further search. We therefore maintain At as a MAP-Elites-style archive
(Mouret & Clune, 2015) holding at most K=50 incumbents, one per niche: a region of structural–
semantic descriptor space within which candidates compete on fitness. Competition within niches
preserves alternatives across descriptor regions, keeping them available for Speculator mutation and
crossover and Navigator synthesis even when they fall outside the global top ranks.
The Embedded population block constructs the descriptors used by the Adaptive archive. Let
r = 1, 2, . . . index successive descriptor-fitting rounds. At each round, we estimate the PCA basis and
standardization parameters from the current archive and hold them fixed until the next refit. Under
the descriptor map fitted at round r, each program is represented as

from the code’s abstract syntax tree (AST), each transformed by log(1 + x) to reduce sensitivity
to unusually large programs. The semantic block captures the strategy description d(p) through its
embedding e(p). We subtract the archive embedding mean ¯er and project onto the eight leading PCA
directions stored in Ur, yielding eight semantic features. The operators Zast

and Zsem

each feature separately by subtracting its archive mean and dividing by its archive standard deviation,
both estimated at fitting round r; features with zero variance are mapped to zero. This makes
the structural and semantic features comparable in scale for the Euclidean distances used in niche
assignment (Appendix D.1).

Figure 2: Overview of SPECEVO. Initialization (left) generates M seed programs, expands each executable
seed into V lightweight variants, and embeds the evaluated population to initialize the archive. During evolution
(right), W lightweight-model Speculators continuously explore the archive. The frontier-model Navigator (top)
intervenes every ∆N completed evaluations, while the lightweight-model Advisor (bottom) updates reusable
guidance every ∆A evaluations.
3.2
THE SPECULATE-THEN-CONSOLIDATE WORKFLOW
While fewer than K slots are occupied, valid candidates are admitted into new slots. At capacity,
the first descriptor fit defines sites ci = zr(pi) whose Voronoi cells form the niches. A candidate
is then assigned to its nearest site and admitted only if it strictly improves that niche’s incumbent.
Replacement leaves the site and descriptor map fixed until the next refit, stabilizing candidate as-
signment. After initialization, every ∆C=50 completed evaluations, we refit PCA and normalization
statistics on the current archive, recompute incumbent descriptors, and re-anchor the sites to follow
the evolving population. Slot indices support progress tracking, although niche boundaries can change
(Appendix D). Table 3 shows the effect of refitting on overall search performance.
4


--- Page 5 ---
Stagnation signal.
The low-to-high scale in the Navigator block represents search stagnation: st
increases toward 1 when either global-best improvements or archive admissions become infrequent.
We use this signal to adjust both parent selection and the scope of Navigator intervention:
st = max

where τ best
t
and τ adm
t
denote the evaluation steps of the most recent global-best improvement
and archive admission, respectively, with normalization horizons Hg=100 and Hl=20. Each term
measures a normalized waiting time, capped at one. Taking their maximum makes st = 1 after 100
evaluations without a global-best improvement or 20 without an archive admission.
Speculators: continuous exploration.
We use W asynchronous Speculators (W=4 in our experi-
ments), which continuously generate candidates using MS. Sampling concentrates on leading elites
when the search is progressing, while increasing stagnation broadens exploration toward lower-ranked
archive regions. Whenever a worker becomes idle, it selects a parent according to its fitness rank ri
under a Zipf distribution whose exponent adapts to stagnation (Piantadosi, 2014):
Pr(pi | At) =
r−βt
i
P|At|
j=1 r−βt
j
,
βt = βmin + (1 −st)(βmax −βmin),
(3)
with (βmin, βmax) = (0.3, 2.0). Thus, βt decreases from 2.0 to 0.3 as stagnation increases, flattening
the distribution while retaining a preference for higher ranks. We use rank-based selection to avoid
dependence on task-specific score scales. The worker then inserts the selected parent into one
of six uniformly sampled variation prompts: general mutation, focused single-weakness repair,
mechanism replacement, analysis-targeted mutation, structural crossover, and component-level
crossover. Figure 8 and Table 3 show that using these complementary prompts sustains higher code
diversity and yields better performance than a single general mutation prompt. For crossover, the
worker draws the second parent from a different niche whenever possible. Every proposal is executed,
checked against the archive admission rule, and recorded in Ht whether or not it is admitted.
Navigator: sparse, state-dependent intervention.
At each Navigator checkpoint, the thresholds
γ1 and γ2 partition the stagnation signal into three levels of increasing intervention scope:
mt =





SYNTHESIS,
st ≤γ1,
SURGICAL,
γ1 < st ≤γ2,
REFRAME,
st > γ2,
(γ1, γ2) = (0.4, 0.7).
(4)
When progress remains steady, the Navigator uses SYNTHESIS to combine complementary mecha-
nisms from competitive niches into a coherent program. Under moderate stagnation, it uses SURGICAL
for a targeted structural correction to the current champion, while under stronger stagnation it uses
REFRAME to introduce a strategy family absent from the current population (Appendix H.2).
The Navigator receives a two-resolution view rather than the full population: complete code for a
few high-ranking niche incumbents and summaries of descriptions and scores from five additional
niches. We use three anchors for SYNTHESIS, the champion alone for SURGICAL, and two anchors
for REFRAME. This view bounds context while exposing behaviorally distinct alternatives without
encouraging verbatim imitation (see Appendix D.3 for details). The Navigator outputs a complete
candidate program and its strategy description, and the program is evaluated immediately. If it is
valid, the Speculators generate J=5 nearby variants, allowing a single expensive intervention to seed
several low-cost follow-up evaluations.
Advisor: consolidating evidence into guidance.
Every ∆A=50 evaluations, the Advisor converts
recent trajectory statistics and accumulated failure information into a compact prescriptive note. Using
Ht and the archive, it identifies working niches whose incumbents improved during the latest interval
and uses saturated to denote niches with high evaluation activity but no incumbent improvement
over the same interval. It also draws on a persistent memory of recurring execution-failure signatures
with representative evaluator messages (Appendix D.4). Based on these signals and its previous
note, the Advisor rewrites guidance of at most 500 words specifying which mechanisms to preserve,
which directions to de-emphasize, and which recurring errors to avoid. The note thus acts as a rolling,

revisable memory rather than an ever-growing transcript. To reduce feedback-induced herding, the

proposals to explore without explicit Advisor guidance.
4
EXPERIMENTS
We address three research questions: RQ1: Does SPECEVO outperform strong LLM-driven evolu-
tionary methods under matched wall-clock, API-cost, and evaluation budgets? RQ2: Does speculate-
then-consolidate outperform cost-efficient strategies exploiting the asymmetry between lightweight
and frontier models? RQ3: How do the Speculator, Navigator, and Advisor individually contribute to
exploration diversity, strategic search progress, and failure reduction?
Benchmarks. We evaluate SPECEVO on 176 real-world scientific and algorithmic discovery tasks
spanning four categories: mathematics (7 problems from AlphaEvolve Math (Novikov et al., 2025)),
systems optimization (4 problems from ADRS (Cheng et al., 2025)), combinatorial optimization (36
problems from CO-Bench (Sun et al., 2026)), and scientific equation discovery (129 problems from
LSR-Synth (Shojaee et al., 2025b)). Detailed benchmark descriptions are provided in Appendix F.
Baselines and setup. Our baselines comprise single-LLM configurations of OpenEvolve (Sharma,
2025), GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2025), AdaEvolve (Cemri et al., 2026), and EvoX (Liu et al.,
2026b), alongside the cost-efficient heterogeneous-model approaches LEVI (Tanveer, 2026) and
RelayEvolve (Luo et al., 2026a). Following RelayEvolve’s evaluation design, we further exam-
ine four controlled model-allocation strategies: All-cheap, which uses only the lightweight model;
Fixed-switch, which uses the lightweight model for the first half of the calls and the frontier model
thereafter; Random, which selects either model with equal probability at each call; and Bandit,
which adaptively selects between the two models using improvements in the best-so-far score as
rewards. Appendix C provides their implementation details. We evaluate frontier proprietary and
open-weight models: GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025) and Kimi-K2-Thinking (hereafter Kimi-K2; Team
et al., 2025), together with four Qwen models ranging from 7B to 30B parameters (Qwen Team,
2025), all accessed through OpenRouter (see Table 9 for prices). Unless otherwise stated, SPECEVO
uses GPT-5 for the Navigator and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 for the Speculators and Advisor.
Experiments run on a dual-socket server with two 16-core Intel Xeon Silver 4314 CPUs, with results
averaged over three independent runs. To ensure a fair comparison under the three-hour wall-clock
budget, we configure baselines with native support for parallel search to use W = 4 workers, while
retaining their original sequential execution schedules otherwise. Section 4.2 reports component
ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses under the same three-hour wall-clock budget. Full
hyperparameters and metric definitions are provided in Appendices D and E, respectively.
4.1
MAIN RESULTS
RQ1: Overall effectiveness.
SPECEVO remains consistently strong across domains, budgets,
and model configurations, supporting the contribution of its search organization across the tested
backbones. Figures 3 and 4 summarize performance under the three-hour wall-clock budget. We
find that SPECEVO leads most mathematical settings and all systems settings, while achieving the
highest aggregate CO-Bench score, 3.8% higher than the strongest competitor, and ranking first on

over 50% of the problems. Across these domains, its API cost is approximately 50%–80% lower
than that of frontier-heavy baselines under the API pricing used in our experiments. Figure 1 further
shows that SPECEVO is robust across the tested frontier and lightweight backbones, whereas
competing methods exhibit performance drops of up to 20% with Qwen3-30B. With GPT-5 as the
frontier model, all small-model variants attain the best score of 0.240 on MinMax 14-3 and the
maximum score of 26.256 on PRISM. Moreover, while several baselines degrade noticeably when
the frontier backbone is changed from GPT-5 to Kimi-K2, SPECEVO remains competitive across
configurations (Appendix G.2). See Appendices G.1–G.3 for detailed results and cost breakdowns.
Figure 5 further shows that SPECEVO reaches stronger solutions earlier and at substantially lower
API cost, whereas other baselines improve more slowly and plateau at lower quality despite greater
expenditure.
Under the $10 API budget, Figure 6 further shows that SPECEVO outperforms the strongest baseline
by shifting routine exploration to inexpensive Speculators and reserving sparse, history-informed
frontier calls for strategic intervention, with the largest improvement observed on LLM-SQL (5.12%
gain). Importantly, Table 2 and Figure 1 (bottom) show that the advantage persists under an identical
budget of 500 evaluations on LSR-Synth. In a separate sample-efficiency analysis, we continue
the baseline trajectories beyond 500 evaluations and measure when they first match SPECEVO’s
performance at evaluation 500. SPECEVO achieves the lowest NMSE across all eight domain–split
settings, while competing methods require approximately 43%–65% more evaluations to reach com-
parable quality. The consistent advantage on OOD data and high symbolic accuracy further suggest
that SPECEVO discovers more generalizable functional structure rather than merely fitting observed
samples. Further breakdowns and statistical significance analyses are provided in Appendix G.4.
RQ2: Heterogeneous model coordination.
SPECEVO’s advantage stems not merely from com-
bining inexpensive and frontier models, but from coordinating their roles using accumulated search
evidence. Table 1 compares coordination strategies under a common budget of 500 model calls. We
find that SPECEVO ranks first on most tasks and never below second, while using the frontier model
for only 2.4% of calls, compared with 89.0% for RelayEvolve. All-cheap omits frontier reasoning,
while Fixed-switch, Random, and Bandit vary model use without the same trajectory-conditioned
coordination. RelayEvolve ends lightweight exploration after a one-way handoff, whereas LEVI
assigns the frontier model primarily to predefined paradigm shifts. SPECEVO instead combines fixed
Navigator checkpoints with stagnation-dependent intervention modes, inexpensive follow-up variants,
and Advisor guidance distilled from search history. Since LEVI also uses a small frontier-call share,
these results suggest that effective coordination depends on how scarce frontier reasoning informs
subsequent search, beyond simply reducing its frequency.

RQ3: Search dynamics.
The search traces on mathematical discovery tasks reveal how the three
roles form a complementary feedback loop. Figure 8 compares population diversity using the Code
Diversity Index (CDI) (Dat et al., 2025). CDI is the entropy of normalized positive edge lengths in
a minimum spanning tree connecting the programs’ code embeddings. Higher values indicate that
separation is distributed more evenly across the population. Because CDI also depends on population
size, we compare methods at checkpoints with comparable archive sizes. SPECEVO maintains higher
CDI than its single-prompt ablation and LEVI as search progresses. Speculators combine stagnation-
adaptive parent sampling with specialized variation prompts to counter lightweight models’ tendency
to repeat familiar structures (Dat et al., 2025). The archive retains distinct strategy families, including
analytic template-based constructions, penalty-annealed search, and neighbor-query-accelerated local
refinement (examples in Appendix I).
Figure 7 summarizes stagnation and frontier-model contribution using statistics computed from the
search traces. We define stagnation rate as the longest consecutive span of evaluations without a new
global best, divided by the total number of evaluations. The reported rate is 17.5% for SPECEVO,
compared with 22.4% for LEVI. Frontier-model contribution measures the fraction of new-best
events produced either directly by the frontier model or by lightweight offspring with a frontier-
generated parent. This fraction is 15.5% for SPECEVO, compared with 10.2% for LEVI, capturing
improvements from both Navigator proposals and their subsequent lightweight refinement. At fixed
checkpoints, the Navigator selects among synthesis, surgical refinement, and reframing according
to stagnation. The annotated examples in Figure 5 illustrate how these interventions change the
search strategy and are followed by further score improvements. It also provides concrete examples
of the Advisor turning execution failures into reusable instructions. On Circle Packing Rectangle,
it recommends explicit nonempty-array checks and clipping radii to at least 10−12. On EPLB, it
recommends scalar Boolean checks and consistent tensor data types. These instructions address
specific causes of rejected candidates, allowing subsequent proposals to retain useful algorithmic
ideas while correcting their implementation. Consistent with this role, Figure 9 shows that SPECEVO
reaches execution error rates of approximately 5%–8%, compared with 13%–25% for LEVI. The
higher error rates of the variant without the Advisor further support the benefit of carrying failure-
related guidance across attempts. Advice is included in only a subset of Speculator prompts, leaving
the remaining proposals free to explore without this guidance.

ABLATION STUDIES
We ablate the speculation and consolidation components of SPECEVO’s StC workflow (Table 3). For
speculation, we remove AST features or description embeddings from the archive descriptor, disable
periodic refits, or replace the six specialized prompts with a single general mutation operator. For
consolidation, we remove the Navigator or replace its adaptive mode selection with random selection
or a fixed mode (Synthesis, Surgical, or Reframe). We also remove the Advisor or replace its evolving
guidance with fixed advice. We further assess sensitivity to the archive capacity K, Navigator and
Advisor intervals, and Speculator count (Figures 11, 12).
Component contributions. Table 3 supports two complementary sources of improvement: diverse
exploration and consolidation that adapts to the search trajectory. Structural and semantic descriptors
preserve distinct implementations and strategies, while periodic refits keep niches aligned with the
evolving population. Specialized Speculator prompts sustain complementary search moves; collaps-
ing them into a single operator produces the largest exploration-side degradation, particularly on
Heilbronn Triangle. The consolidation ablations highlight the importance of conditioning feedback
on search state. Random Navigator modes underperform on both tasks, while the strongest fixed
mode differs across tasks, supporting the value of matching intervention scope to stagnation. Fixed
guidance likewise underperforms adaptive Advisor updates and even yields lower mean performance
than removing the Advisor on Heilbronn Triangle. This suggests that static advice can become coun-
terproductive as the search evolves, motivating continual revision based on productive mechanisms,
saturated directions, and recurring failures.
Case studies. Figure 5 illustrates this division of labor, while Figure 10 shows the final packing
solutions. On Circle Packing Rectangle, routine refinement initially concentrates on similar geometric
constructions. The Navigator then uses REFRAME to introduce simulated annealing with geometric
repair and, later, gradient-enhanced scaling with backtracking line search. The Advisor complements
these shifts with safeguards for empty arrays and near-zero radii, allowing subsequent Speculator
variants to explore the new neighborhoods without repeatedly failing on numerical edge cases. A
similar pattern appears on EPLB: SURGICAL first strengthens the incumbent through Huntington–
Hill apportionment and load-aware heap scheduling, while REFRAME later replaces the saturated
placement logic with load-to-count allocation and rotated round-robin assignment. Between these
interventions, the Advisor helps prevent recurring dtype and scalar-boolean errors. These interventions
provide reusable starting points for continued low-cost Speculator refinement.
Hyperparameter sensitivity. In Figure 11, we find that K = 50 yields the strongest performance,
suggesting a balance between strategy coverage and sufficient refinement within each niche. The

Figure 12: Effect of the number of Speculators

preferred Navigator and Advisor intervals are 20 and 50 evaluations, respectively. This difference is
consistent with their informational needs: strategic intervention benefits from timely responses to
stagnation, whereas reusable guidance requires enough observations to distinguish recurring patterns
from isolated outcomes. Figure 12 shows that scaling from one to four Speculators improves both
solution quality and evaluation throughput on Circle Packing. Beyond four, throughput continues
to increase, but quality gains become marginal while token usage and API cost rise sharply. We
therefore use four Speculators to capture most of the benefit of parallel exploration at moderate cost.
5
CONCLUSION
We introduced SPECEVO, a multi-LLM framework that coordinates low-cost exploration and sparse
frontier-model reasoning through continual consolidation of search evidence. Its speculate-then-
consolidate workflow combines parallel lightweight Speculators, persistent Advisor guidance distilled
from successes, failures, and saturated directions, and stagnation-dependent Navigator interventions
at fixed checkpoints. Across 176 scientific and algorithmic discovery tasks, SPECEVO matches
or outperforms strong baselines under matched wall-clock, API-cost, and evaluation budgets, with
50%–80% lower API expenditure under the three-hour wall-clock budget. Its gains across backbone
configurations and under matched evaluation budgets support the value of using accumulated search
evidence to guide sparse frontier interventions and subsequent lightweight refinement.
AI USE STATEMENT
LLMs in the method and evaluation.
LLMs are a core component of the method studied in this
work. SPECEVO and all baselines call the language models listed in Table 9 to generate, refine, and an-
alyze candidate programs (Section 4 and Appendix C), and we use text-embedding-3-small
for SPECEVO’s archive descriptors and for the diversity metric (Appendices D and E). To score
symbolic accuracy on LSR-Synth, we follow the LLM-SRBench protocol (Shojaee et al., 2025b) and
use GPT-4o to judge whether a discovered equation is mathematically equivalent to the ground truth
(Appendix G.4). These uses are part of the experimental method and evaluation protocol described in
the paper.
AI assistance in research and writing.
We used generative AI tools to assist with writing, including
language editing, improving clarity and readability, and condensing or rephrasing parts of the
manuscript. The authors reviewed and revised all AI-assisted text. We take responsibility for the final
content of this work, including text, claims, or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Appendix
This appendix provides supplementary material supporting the methodology, evaluation, and analysis presented
in the main paper. Appendix A discusses the limitations of SPECEVO. Appendices B and C extend the
related-work discussion and document the baselines and common evaluation protocol. Appendix D provides the
complete algorithmic specification of SPECEVO, including the Speculator loop and the Navigator and Advisor
interventions, while Appendix E defines the metrics used to analyze search dynamics. Appendices F and G
describe the benchmark suites and provide detailed experimental results, including API cost and token usage
breakdowns. Appendix H presents the complete prompt templates for all three roles, and Appendix I analyzes
generated programs, recurring failure modes, algorithmic mechanisms, and the guidance consolidated by the
Advisor on Circle Packing Rectangle and EPLB.

A
LIMITATIONS
Dependence on parallel computing infrastructure.
The wall-clock efficiency of SPECEVO partly
depends on the amount of parallelism available to the Speculator pool. Our experiments use W = 4
concurrent Speculators on a dual-socket server with two 16-core Intel Xeon Silver 4314 processors.
Consequently, the number of candidates explored within a fixed wall-clock budget may change with
the worker count, CPU capacity, memory bandwidth, network latency, and API rate limits. Although
our fixed API-cost and fixed evaluation-budget experiments provide complementary controls, they
do not make the wall-clock results hardware-independent. The reported cost reductions should
therefore be interpreted primarily as savings in LLM API expenditure under the specified computing
environment, rather than reductions in total computational cost.
Compute-intensive candidate evaluation.
The benchmarks considered in this work use relatively
lightweight evaluators: candidate programs can generally be executed and scored on CPUs without re-
peatedly training large neural networks, running long simulations, or conducting physical experiments.
This setting allows multiple Speculators to evaluate proposals concurrently at modest local-compute
cost. For tasks whose evaluation requires GPU training, large-scale inference, expensive simulation,
or real-world experimentation, increasing the number of parallel workers may instead multiply
accelerator usage, memory requirements, and the cost of unsuccessful trials. Moreover, a fixed
number of evaluations does not represent a fixed compute budget when candidate evaluations have
heterogeneous costs. Evaluating SPECEVO in such settings is an important direction for future work.
A more comprehensive study should jointly control API expenditure, CPU- or GPU-hours, peak
memory, energy consumption, wall-clock time, and the number of evaluated candidates. It would
also be valuable to adapt the worker count and the frequencies of Navigator and Advisor intervention
dynamically according to evaluator cost, available hardware, and observed search progress.
Reliability of model-generated descriptions.
The semantic component of our archive descriptor
relies on descriptions produced by the proposing model, predominantly lightweight Speculators.
These descriptions may omit important changes, remain generic across distinct programs, or claim
mechanisms absent from the code. Such inaccuracies can distort semantic distances, grouping
different strategies together or separating similar implementations, thereby affecting niche assignment,
parent selection, and the population summaries provided to the Navigator and Advisor. We have not
systematically quantified sensitivity to description quality. Future work could evaluate this sensitivity
through controlled description perturbations and explore code-grounded verification or descriptors
derived from execution behavior.
B
EXTENDED RELATED WORK
LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search.
LLM-guided evolutionary search combines language mod-
els as semantic variation operators with executable evaluators and population-based optimiza-
tion. FunSearch established this paradigm by evolving programs for open mathematical prob-
lems (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), while ELM combined pretrained code models with quality-
diversity search (Lehman et al., 2023). Subsequent methods specialize the evolutionary loop in
different ways: EoH jointly evolves natural-language ideas and executable heuristics (Liu et al.,
2024b); ReEvo derives reflective guidance from performance comparisons (Ye et al., 2024); LLaMEA
evolves optimization algorithms through iterative evaluation (Van Stein & B¨ack, 2024); HSEvo
explicitly balances diversity and convergence (Dat et al., 2025); and MPaGE extends heuristic
evolution to multiple objectives (Hieu et al., 2026). Related systems apply LLM-guided search to
reward design (Ma et al., 2024b), preference optimization (Lu et al., 2024), and scientific equation
discovery (Li et al., 2026; Shojaee et al., 2025b;a; Grayeli et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024a). More general
evolutionary coding agents include AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025),
and ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), while GEPA evolves prompts and natural-language rules
through reflection and Pareto selection (Agrawal et al., 2025). Recent work further improves the
representation and control of search: SeaEvo organizes candidates into persistent semantic strategy
families (Luo et al., 2026b); EvoX evolves the search strategy itself (Liu et al., 2026b); AdaEvolve
adapts exploration intensity, resource allocation across islands, and meta-level guidance (Cemri et al.,
2026); and CORAL delegates search decisions to autonomous peer agents communicating through
shared memory (Qu et al., 2026). Unlike these systems, SPECEVO assigns routine exploration,
15


--- Page 16 ---
experience consolidation, and strategic intervention to models of different cost, analogous to the
division of labor in a research laboratory.
Cost-Aware LLM Routing and Evolutionary Search Allocation.
Cost-aware LLM systems
reduce inference expense by selecting among models with different capabilities. FrugalGPT con-
structs cascades that progressively escalate difficult queries (Chen et al., 2023b), AutoMix uses
self-verification to decide whether a small-model response requires augmentation by a stronger
model (Aggarwal et al., 2024), and RouteLLM learns routing policies from human preference
data (Ong et al., 2025). These methods focus on independent inference requests, whereas evo-
lutionary search must allocate resources across a sequence of interdependent population updates.
ShinkaEvolve addresses this setting with a bandit that selects mutation models according to their
observed performance (Lange et al., 2026). AdaptEvolve instead runs a small model first and uses
token-level confidence statistics with an online decision-tree router to determine whether the mutation
should be regenerated by a larger model (Ray et al., 2026). AdaEvolve allocates computation across
concurrent evolutionary processes according to their recent progress and introduces meta-level rea-
soning to adjust search behavior under stagnation (Cemri et al., 2026). RelayEvolve shifts allocation
from individual mutations to entire search phases: a cheap model develops multiple trajectories in
short blocks, Relay Gain measures the marginal quality and coverage of their candidate bank, and
saturation of this signal triggers a one-time handoff of a curated seed population to strong-model
evolution (Luo et al., 2026a). LEVI combines three complementary mechanisms: bootstrapped
CVT-MAP-Elites for diversity preservation, role-aware routing that assigns local refinements to
smaller models and paradigm shifts to a stronger model, and rank-preserving proxy benchmarks that
reduce evaluation overhead (Tanveer, 2026).
These approaches optimize different components of resource allocation but retain important structural
restrictions. ShinkaEvolve and AdaptEvolve select among models at the mutation level, leaving
them functionally interchangeable; AdaptEvolve additionally requires token-level probabilities that
are unavailable from many proprietary APIs. AdaEvolve adapts the amount and direction of search
effort but does not organize heterogeneous models into persistent functional roles. RelayEvolve
captures population-level state more explicitly, but information flows through a single cheap-to-
strong transition: once handoff occurs, lightweight exploration ends, and the strong phase inherits
selected candidates but no consolidated knowledge about discarded attempts, recurring failures, or
exhausted trajectories. LEVI provides a clearer division between local and structural mutations, but
its stronger model is assigned primarily to a predefined paradigm-shift operation, without a dedicated
component that continually aggregates trajectory-wide evidence for subsequent small-model search.
SPECEVO instead treats model heterogeneity as a persistent division of labor throughout evolution.
Its Speculators perform high-throughput variation, its Advisor repeatedly converts successes, failures,
and niche-level progress into reusable guidance, and its Navigator examines the population at sparse
checkpoints to choose among synthesis, surgical refinement, and reframing. Where prior methods
optimize model selection, phase transition, or mutation type, SPECEVO coordinates candidate
generation, experience consolidation, and strategic intervention within the same evolutionary process.
C
BASELINE DETAILS
Common evaluation protocol.
We evaluate all baselines using their native search logic and publicly
released implementations. We introduce only the task adapters required to expose the same problem
specification, editable program scaffold, execution environment, and evaluator to every method. All
three-hour wall-clock experiments use the same hardware and evaluation environment. For baseline
implementations supporting native parallel candidate search, we configure four concurrent workers,
matching SPECEVO. The wall-clock results therefore characterize end-to-end performance under this
protocol, complemented by comparisons under fixed API-cost and evaluation budgets.
All initialization, mutation, repair, reflection, meta-guidance, and paradigm-shift calls are included in
API-cost and wall-clock accounting. API expenditure is computed from the actual input and output
tokens of each call using the prices in Table 9. Under an evaluation budget, every candidate submitted
to the evaluator consumes one evaluation, including programs that fail to parse, violate constraints,
or time out; auxiliary calls that do not produce a candidate do not increment this counter but still
contribute to API cost and elapsed time. Under the 500-call RQ2 budget, every LLM invocation
16


--- Page 17 ---
counts toward the common limit. Each method returns the highest-scoring valid program discovered
before its stopping condition is reached.
OpenEvolve.
OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025) implements asynchronous island-based program evo-
lution with a MAP-Elites-style database. Candidate parents are selected from a mixture of high-
performing and behaviorally diverse programs, mutated using evaluator feedback, and periodically
exchanged across islands. We retain its native archive, migration, and prompt construction mecha-
nisms, while assigning the selected frontier backbone to all LLM calls.
GEPA.
We use the inference-time code-optimization configuration of GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2025),
treating the candidate program as the textual artifact being optimized. GEPA converts execution
traces and evaluator diagnostics into natural-language reflection, uses the resulting analysis to propose
targeted mutations, and maintains complementary candidates through Pareto-aware selection and
merging. The same frontier backbone is used for both reflection and candidate generation.
AdaEvolve.
AdaEvolve (Cemri et al., 2026) derives an accumulated-improvement signal from
the search trajectory and uses it at three levels: adjusting exploration intensity within each island,
allocating evaluations across islands through a bandit scheduler, and generating new high-level
tactics when global progress stalls. We use the authors’ released implementation and default adaptive
schedules, with the designated frontier backbone serving both mutation and meta-guidance calls.
EvoX.
EvoX (Liu et al., 2026b) jointly evolves candidate programs and the strategy used to
generate them. Its inner loop evaluates programs under the current search strategy, while its outer
loop periodically revises parent selection and variation behavior according to the progress achieved
during the preceding search window. We preserve this two-level evolution and use the same frontier
backbone for solution generation and search-strategy evolution.
LEVI.
LEVI (Tanveer, 2026) first generates diverse seeds to calibrate a CVT-MAP-Elites archive
and then applies role-aware model routing. Qwen3-30B performs ordinary local refinements, whereas
the frontier model is reserved for periodically triggered paradigm shifts conditioned on representatives
from distinct archive regions. We retain its native archive descriptors, trigger policy, lightweight
follow-up variants, and proxy-benchmark construction where applicable. All reported final programs
are re-evaluated using the complete task evaluator.
RelayEvolve.
RelayEvolve (Luo et al., 2026a) begins with multiple lightweight-model trajectories
whose search blocks are allocated by a Grow–Deepen bandit. Relay Gain measures the marginal
quality and coverage contributed to an online candidate bank and triggers handoff when further
cheap-model exploration saturates. The terminal candidate pool is then curated using the method’s
quality–diversity objective, and the selected population initializes a shared frontier-model search
using the remaining budget. We retain the default strong-model budget reserve and all handoff
hyperparameters. Once handoff occurs, lightweight-model exploration does not resume.
Controlled model-allocation strategies.
To isolate the effect of model coordination from the
mere availability of two differently priced models, we additionally implement four controls on a
shared asynchronous evolutionary backend. They use identical parent selection, population updates,
mutation prompts, evaluator feedback, and context limits, differing only in how the lightweight and
frontier models are assigned. For a total call budget B, these strategies are defined as follows:
• All-cheap assigns every call to the lightweight model.
• Fixed-switch uses the lightweight model for the first B/2 calls and then performs a one-time
switch to the frontier model for the remaining calls, carrying the current population forward
without additional curation.
• Random independently selects the lightweight or frontier model with probability 0.5 for
every call.
• Bandit treats the two models as arms of a UCB1 scheduler. After initializing both arms,
model selection balances their observed mean rewards with an exploration bonus. The
reward is the non-negative improvement in the global best score produced by the selected
model; invalid or non-improving proposals receive zero reward.
17


--- Page 18 ---
D
ALGORITHM DETAILS
We set the temperatures to 0.5, 0.5, and 0.8 for the synthesis, surgical, and reframe modes, respec-
tively, and to 0.7 and 0.4 for the Speculator and Advisor. We set Hg = 100, Hl = 20, βmin = 0.3,
βmax = 2.0, γ1 = 0.4, and γ2 = 0.7. We refit the archive descriptor space every ∆C = 50 completed
evaluations, setting ∆C = ∆A for consistency with the Advisor update interval. After each Navigator
call generates a set of hypotheses, the Speculators produce J = 5 variants for each hypothesis.
D.1
BEHAVIORAL DESCRIPTOR CONSTRUCTION
We provide the implementation details of the structural–semantic descriptor introduced in Eq. 1. For
a program p, we first parse its source code into a Python abstract syntax tree and extract the following
eight statistics, in fixed order:
a(p) = [ adepth, acyc, aloop, anest, abranch, afunc, acomp, acall ].
These denote the maximum AST depth; cyclomatic complexity; the number of For and While nodes;
the maximum nesting depth of such loops; and the numbers of If, FunctionDef, comprehension,
and function-call nodes, respectively. Cyclomatic complexity is initialized to one, incremented for
each If, While, For, and ExceptHandler, and additionally incremented by the Boolean fan-out
of each BoolOp. To reduce the influence of unusually large programs, we apply an element-wise
logarithmic transform,
ϕ(p) = log
␀1 + a(p)

∈R8.
As a defensive fallback, an unparsable program is assigned an all-zero structural vector, although
such programs are normally rejected before archive admission.
For the semantic block, we embed the model-generated strategy description d(p) using text-
embedding-3-small. The resulting 1536-dimensional vector is L2-normalized:
e(p) =
femb(d(p))
max{∥femb(d(p))∥2, ε} ∈R1536.
The raw embedding is computed once for each distinct description and cached; refits therefore do not
require additional embedding calls.
At refit round r, let Ar be the current archive and let ¯er be the mean of its description embeddings.
We fit PCA to the centered embedding matrix and retain the leading eight principal directions,
Ur ∈R1536×8. The semantic representation is
qr(p) = U ⊤

␀e(p) −¯er

∈R8.
The structural and semantic blocks are standardized separately, coordinate by coordinate, using their
respective means and standard deviations over the current archive. A coordinate with zero empirical
variance is mapped to zero. The final descriptor is the direct concatenation
zr(p) =

Zast

r
(qr(p))

∈R16,
where ∥denotes concatenation. We apply no additional block weighting or normalization after
concatenation; separate standardization prevents either block from dominating the Euclidean geometry
used for niche assignment. The archive holds at most K = 50 incumbents. Rather than partitioning
the population with a separate clustering step, we anchor each niche at its own incumbent: niche i
is the Voronoi cell of the site ci = zr(pi) ∈R16, so the tessellation is determined entirely by the
archive contents under the current descriptor map zr.
Before the first refit, no descriptor map has been fitted and niche assignment does not use one: each
admitted program simply opens a new niche, in admission order. This is the regime in which the
initialization seeds and their lightweight variants enter the archive, so initialization requires neither a
PCA basis nor a set of sites. The first refit is triggered as soon as the archive first holds K incumbents,
which, since M · V ≫K, occurs during the lightweight diversification stage, and establishes z1
together with the initial sites {ci}K
i=1.
Between refit events, zr and the sites {ci} are held fixed. An incoming candidate q is projected using
the most recent PCA basis and normalization statistics and assigned to i⋆= arg mini∥zr(q) −ci∥2.
18


--- Page 19 ---
It is admitted if and only if F(q) > F(pi⋆), in which case it replaces pi⋆but does not displace ci⋆;
the site moves only at the next refit. The archive therefore remains saturated at K occupied niches for
the remainder of the run.
After initialization, every ∆C = 50 completed evaluations we refit PCA on the current archive,
refresh the per-coordinate normalization statistics, rebuild the descriptors zr(pi) of all incumbents,
and re-anchor every site to its incumbent, ci ←zr(pi). Because the sites are the incumbents, a refit
changes only the geometry used to route future candidates: it never merges two incumbents into a
single niche, except in the degenerate case of two identical descriptors, where the higher-scoring
program is retained, and niche index i continues to denote the same archive slot across refits. This
preserves the per-niche statistics the Advisor uses to identify working and saturated niches, and it
removes any need to seed the new geometry with the previous round’s sites, whose coordinates are in
any case no longer comparable once the PCA basis and normalization statistics have been refit.
D.2
THE COMPLETE SPECEVO WORKFLOW
Algorithm 1 illustrates the overall workflow of SPECEVO. Initialization first uses a small number of
frontier-model calls to obtain a diverse set of executable strategy families. Lightweight variants then
expand these seeds into a sufficiently broad population for constructing the behavioral archive. After
initialization, W asynchronous Speculators perform nearly all candidate generation, while the two
consolidation routines are triggered on independent evaluation schedules. Importantly, Navigator
interventions are non-blocking in our implementation: once a Navigator checkpoint is triggered, the
intervention is dispatched as a background task, while the Speculator workers continue generating
and evaluating candidates. Navigator-generated candidates and their lightweight follow-up variants
are incorporated into the shared search state as they complete. Thus, the NAVIGATOR and ADVISOR
calls in Algorithm 1 are written as single operations for notational compactness and should not be
interpreted as synchronization barriers for the Speculator workers.
Speculator step.
Let the archive programs be ordered by decreasing score, with ri denoting the
rank of pi. At each worker step, the parent distribution and its stagnation-dependent exponent are:
Pr(pi | At) =
r−βt
i
P|At|
j=1 r−βt
j
,
βt = βmin + (1 −st)(βmax −βmin).
(5)
For crossover, the second parent is drawn from a different niche whenever possible. Additional
inspirations are sampled without replacement from the same rank distribution after excluding the
parent(s), but only their descriptions and scores are shown. This distinction is intentional: parent
code supplies a concrete object to modify, whereas description-only inspirations broaden the idea set
without encouraging verbatim copying or inflating the prompt.
The six variation prompts are general mutation, focused single-weakness repair, mechanism replace-
ment, analysis-targeted mutation, structural crossover, and component-level crossover. They are
sampled uniformly, so each prompt is used with equal probability during Speculator generation.
Asynchrony and checkpoint cadence.
The evaluation index t counts completed candidate eval-
uations rather than optimizer “generations.” Because Speculators run asynchronously, multiple
evaluations may complete between periodic checks, so a trigger can occur slightly after its nominal
interval. After initialization, the Navigator, Advisor, and archive periodic refits maintain indepen-
dent clocks tN, tA, and tC, all reset to the current t. They are subsequently invoked whenever
t −tN ≥∆N, t −tA ≥∆A, and t −tC ≥∆C, respectively. Thus, initialization does not consume
any of these intervals, and each periodic operation proceeds independently according to its own
evaluation cadence.

The highest-ranked elites are selected as anchors, for which the Navigator observes the complete
program, strategy description, and score. The subsequent elites are used as inspirations, exposing
only their descriptions and scores. Anchors and inspirations are disjoint within each invocation.
Full-code anchors support precise reasoning and modification, whereas description-only inspirations
expose a broader set of mechanisms without overwhelming the prompt; ranking niche elites rather
than the entire population keeps this context behaviorally diverse.
Table 4 summarizes the mode-specific context: SYNTHESIS needs several anchors’ implementations to
combine complementary mechanisms, SURGICAL needs only the champion it repairs, and REFRAME
uses two anchors to identify shared assumptions while relying on descriptions to seek a qualitatively
different strategy family.

Table 4: Mode-specific context provided to the Navigator.
Tracking niche activity and progress.
At each Advisor checkpoint, we inspect the evaluations
completed since the previous checkpoint. For every occupied niche k, we maintain two signals:
an activity count ak, equal to the number of evaluated candidates assigned to that niche during the
interval, and a movement indicator mk, which records whether the niche incumbent was replaced
during the same interval. Importantly, the activity count includes unsuccessful candidates. Hence, a
niche can receive substantial search effort without producing a better incumbent.
These signals distinguish productive search from saturation without requiring a task-specific im-
provement threshold. A niche with recent incumbent movement is treated as actively improving,
whereas a niche with high activity but no movement is considered saturated. This distinction is
particularly useful across our heterogeneous benchmarks, where the scale of score improvements
varies substantially between tasks.
At each checkpoint, the Advisor constructs two complementary population views:
• Dwork

▷break ties by recency
6: Xt ←(Dwork
t
, Dsat
t
, Et, ℓ, ybest
t
, st)
7: ℓ∼MA(· | T , Xt)
▷distill structured guidance
8: return ℓ
• Dsat
t : up to three most active niches that received evaluations but showed no incumbent
movement.
Together, these views separate current solution quality from recent search progress and exploration
coverage. In particular, a high-scoring niche need not be improving, while a lower-scoring niche may
reveal a productive direction that has only recently emerged.
Failure memory. We aggregate evaluator failures from the complete search history Ht, including
initialization, using normalized error signatures. For each signature, Rt records its cumulative
occurrence count, most recent occurrence, and a representative message. No signatures are evicted
during a run. At each Advisor checkpoint, we select the eight most frequent signatures, breaking ties
by recency. This bounds the failure evidence included in the prompt while retaining earlier failures
in the underlying history. The Advisor combines this evidence with recent niche activity and its
previous guidance to revise the next note.
Advisor output and guidance injection.
The Advisor converts the population views, recurrent
failures, and previous advice into a compact note with three fields. WORKING summarizes mecha-
nisms associated with leading or recently improving niches; SATURATED identifies directions that
continue to consume evaluations without moving their incumbents; and AVOID highlights recurrent
anti-patterns supported by the failure memory.
We use temperature 0.4 and a 1000-token generation limit, with the resulting note constrained
to fewer than 500 words. The note is not imposed on every worker. Instead, each subsequent
Speculator receives it independently with probability ρA = 0.35. This stochastic injection allows
useful population-level lessons to propagate through the search while preserving a substantial fraction
of independent exploration.

E.1
AGGREGATE METRICS USED IN FIGURE 3

panel, and ¯sc,t and ¯uc,t the final best score and the API cost (USD) of configuration c on task t, each

E.2
CODE DIVERSITY INDEX (CDI)
CDI (Dat et al., 2025) measures how evenly the population’s code representations are separated along
a minimum spanning tree (MST). At checkpoint t, let Qt = {p1, . . . , pn} be the complete archive
snapshot. We first canonicalize each source string. For each Python program, we parse its abstract
syntax tree, remove comments and module/function/class docstrings, and emit a deterministically
formatted program. If parsing fails, we fall back to whitespace-normalized source. Let
xi = femb(canon(code(pi))) ∈Rd
(6)
be the embedding of the resulting code. We use text-embedding-3-small for all methods
and checkpoints.
Construct the complete undirected graph on the n embeddings with Euclidean edge weight
dij = ∥xi −xj∥2.
(7)
Let EMST
t
be the edge set of a minimum spanning tree, and let E+
t = {e ∈EMST
t
: de > 0} remove
zero-length duplicate edges. Normalize its positive edge lengths as
πe =
de
P
e′∈E+
t de′ .
(8)
The reported Code Diversity Index is the Shannon entropy
CDI(Qt) = −
X
e∈E+
t
πe log πe,
(9)
where log is the natural logarithm. If there is no positive MST edge (e.g., n ≤1 or all embeddings
coincide), CDI is defined as zero.
CDI is high when separation is distributed across many MST edges instead of being dominated by
one bridge between otherwise collapsed groups. Since the edge lengths are normalized, uniform
rescaling of every embedding distance does not change CDI; the metric captures the distribution of
population separations, not an absolute diameter. With m = |E+
t | ≥1 positive edges, 0 ≤CDI ≤
log m ≤log(n −1), with the upper bound attained when the positive MST edges have equal length.
Because this upper bound depends on population size, comparisons should use checkpoints with
comparable archive sizes. Our computation keeps duplicate programs by default and uses the archive
exactly as stored at the checkpoint.
E.3
STAGNATION RATE
The reported stagnation rate is a post-hoc, run-level statistic that asks what fraction of the full
evaluation budget was consumed by the single longest global-best plateau.
For a run of T evaluations, define the new-best index set
Ibest =


1≤j<t yj

= {b1 < · · · < bm}.
(10)
Set the sentinels b0 = 0 and bm+1 = T + 1. The number of consecutive non-new-best evaluations
between two adjacent events is gi = bi+1 −bi −1. This convention includes the prefix before the
first new best and the suffix after the last new best. The run-level metric is
StagRate = 100 × max0≤i≤m gi
T
(%).

E.4
NEW BESTS TRACED TO THE FRONTIER MODEL
This metric measures how often observed progress can be attributed to the frontier model. In
LEVI, the frontier model is invoked through paradigm shift, while in SPECEVO it serves as
the Navigator. For each new-best event bi in Eq. 10, define
z(bi) =



1,
if bi is generated by the frontier model, or by a small model
with at least one frontier-generated parent,
0,
otherwise.
(12)

The run-level rate is
FrontierTrace = 100 ×
Pm
i=1 z(bi)
m
(%),
(13)
where m is the number of new-best events. Thus, FrontierTrace measures the fraction of improve-
ments that are either directly produced by the frontier model or arise from lightweight refinement of
its programs. Initialization is excluded, and the metric is reported as missing when m = 0. Since it
counts improvement events rather than their magnitude, it should be interpreted together with final
performance and API cost.
F
BENCHMARK DETAILS
We provide additional details about the benchmarks used in our evaluation. Unless otherwise stated, a
candidate solution is represented as an executable program and evaluated by a task-specific evaluator.
The evolutionary methods only observe the resulting scalar score and diagnostic feedback, without
access to hidden test instances or ground-truth solutions.
F.1
MATHEMATICAL OPTIMIZATION BENCHMARKS
We consider seven executable mathematical optimization tasks covering geometric packing, extremal
point configurations, and signal processing. The geometric tasks follow the formulations used in
AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025). Each candidate program constructs or refines a feasible solution,
and the evaluator returns a scalar higher-is-better objective value. The exact configurations used in
our experiments are summarized in Table 5.
F.2
SYSTEMS OPTIMIZATION BENCHMARKS
We use four real-world systems optimization tasks from the AI-Driven Research for Systems bench-
mark suite (Cheng et al., 2025). Although some underlying objectives are naturally formulated as
minimization problems, the task evaluators convert them into scalar scores for which a larger value
indicates a better candidate in all reported experiments. Table 6 summarizes the four tasks included
in our evaluation.
F.3
CO-BENCH
CO-Bench (Sun et al., 2026) evaluates the ability of language-model agents to design complete
algorithms for combinatorial optimization rather than directly predicting solutions to individual
instances. It contains 36 real-world optimization problems spanning eight categories and a broad
range of problem sizes and constraint structures. Most instances are curated from OR-Library and
related operations-research collections.
For each problem, the benchmark provides the agent with a natural language problem specification, a
starter solve interface, and a development set. A hidden evaluation function checks feasibility and
measures solution quality. The test instances and evaluator implementation are unavailable during
search, reducing direct overfitting to the final evaluation data.
Let h(x; p) denote the raw objective value of a feasible solution x on instance p, and let h∗
p denote
the reference value recorded in the benchmark. We use the task-specific normalization implemented
in CO-Bench, denoted by Np, to obtain a higher-is-better score:
s(x, p) =
Np
␀h(x; p), h∗
p

,
if execution succeeds and x is feasible,
0,
if execution fails, times out, or x is infeasible.
(14)
For standard positive-reference ratio normalization, Np(h, h∗
p) = h/h∗
p for maximization and
Np(h, h∗
p) = h∗
p/h for minimization, with nonzero denominators. We retain the benchmark’s
special-case handling, including shifted ratios for zero-reference instances.
The normalized score is always interpreted as higher-is-better, regardless of the original optimization
direction. Failed evaluations receive a final normalized score of 0; this value is not substituted into
the raw objective before normalization. A score of 1 corresponds to matching the reference, while

F.4
LSR-SYNTH
We use LSR-Synth from LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025b), a benchmark designed to evaluate
LLM-based scientific equation discovery. Unlike traditional symbolic regression benchmarks that
often contain well-established canonical equations (La Cava et al., 2021; Matsubara et al., 2022),
LSR-Synth combines known functional terms with novel synthetic terms. This construction reduces
the likelihood that models can solve the tasks through memorization or direct recall of equations
encountered during pre-training.
Each problem provides a scientific context, descriptions of the relevant variables, and an observational
dataset. The objective is to discover a mathematical expression that accurately captures the underlying
relationship between the input variables and the target quantity. LSR-Synth covers four scientific
domains: chemistry, biology, physics, and material science.
We use all 129 problems from LSR-Synth, comprising 36 chemistry problems, 24 biology problems,
44 physics problems, and 25 material science problems.
During the search process, candidate equations are ranked using
Score = log10

G
ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
G.1
BREAKDOWN OF API COST AND TOKEN USAGE
Table 9 reports the OpenRouter list prices of all models used in our experiments, and Figure 13
shows the corresponding input and output token usage on six representative tasks with GPT-5 as
the frontier-model backbone. SPECEVO often uses more tokens in total than several baselines, and
in some cases more than LEVI, because it hands a large volume of routine search, mutation, and
refinement to lightweight Speculators. Higher token usage does not mean higher cost: most of the
additional tokens come from inexpensive small models, and costly frontier-model calls are reserved
for infrequent Navigator interventions. With GPT-5 output tokens at $10.00 per million versus $0.30
for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, moving most of the search workload to lightweight models
yields substantial savings even when the total token count is larger.
Tables 10 and 11 provide the task-level API expenditure under the fixed three-hour wall-clock
budget. Excluding LEVI, SPECEVO reduces API cost by approximately 49.9%–70.7% across
the four benchmark–backbone settings. We treat LEVI separately because it also mixes models:
it uses a lightweight model for routine search and calls the frontier model only for occasional
paradigm shift operations, so it already benefits from the same price gap between lightweight
and frontier models. The comparison with LEVI therefore more directly reflects how each method
allocates scarce frontier-model reasoning.
G.2
DETAILED RESULTS FOR MATHEMATICAL DISCOVERY AND SYSTEMS OPTIMIZATION
TASKS
The results below break down the aggregate trends in Figure 3 by task and backbone configuration.
Beyond final performance, we check whether the gains persist when either the frontier model or the
lightweight Speculator is changed, which separates the contribution of the search architecture from
that of any particular model.

Mathematical discovery.
Across both frontier backbones, SPECEVO attains the strongest or tied-
best single-run result on six of the seven tasks and the leading or tied mean performance on five. Its
advantage is most consistent on the Heilbronn and MinMax problems, whose landscapes contain
multiple structurally distinct solution families and densely populated local optima. The adaptive
archive preserves these alternatives, and the Navigator can synthesize promising mechanisms or
reframe the search once lightweight refinement saturates. Even smaller Speculators therefore often
match the strongest configurations on these tasks. Signal Processing is the main exception: its noisy
evaluation makes short-term progress less reliable, so results vary more across lightweight backbones
and conventional baselines remain competitive.
Systems optimization.
The gains are more uniform on systems tasks, where at least one SPECEVO
configuration achieves the best or tied-best mean performance on every problem under both GPT-5
and Kimi-K2. No single lightweight backbone dominates: Qwen3-30B performs strongest on EPLB
and LLM-SQL with GPT-5, Qwen3-14B leads Transaction Scheduling, and Qwen3-8B becomes
strongest on Transaction Scheduling with Kimi-K2. Even Qwen2.5-7B reaches the performance
ceiling on PRISM. This non-monotonic relationship with model size suggests that the gains do not

come simply from a more capable Speculator. In the closed-loop workflow, inexpensive models with
different strengths carry out high-volume refinement, and population-level evidence determines when
strategic redirection is needed.
Robustness and cost efficiency.
This division of labor also reduces sensitivity to the frontier
backbone. Several frontier-only baselines degrade substantially when GPT-5 is replaced by Kimi-
K2, particularly on PRISM, whereas SPECEVO stays close to the task ceiling because the frontier
model acts through sparse, high-impact interventions instead of shaping every mutation. The same
organization reduces API expenditure by 34%–85% on mathematical discovery and 51%–71% on
systems optimization relative to the four frontier-heavy baselines. SPECEVO also generally improves
upon LEVI at comparable cost, which indicates that the remaining quality difference comes mainly
from how scarce frontier reasoning and accumulated evidence are integrated into the search, not from
the model price gap alone.

G.3
DETAILED RESULTS FOR EACH CO-BENCH PROBLEM CATEGORY
Figure 14 summarizes performance across the eight CO-Bench categories, while Table 14 reports
the complete results for all 36 problems. SPECEVO achieves the highest category-level score in five
categories—Packing, Cutting, Scheduling, Routing, and Tree—with the largest advantages observed
on Cutting and Tree problems. At the problem level, SPECEVO ranks first on 20/36 problems, with
strong results on assortment, Euclidean Steiner, flow-shop scheduling, and periodic vehicle-routing
problems. Assignment is nearly saturated across methods, and results on Facility Location are more
mixed.
Figure 15 and Table 15 further examine whether these gains are consistent across individual problems.
The mean paired score difference is positive against every baseline, ranging from +0.0332 against
LEVI to +0.0500 against OpenEvolve, and SPECEVO wins more problems than it loses in all five
pairwise comparisons. The bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean difference are also positive
for four of the five baselines, with AdaEvolve being the exception.

G.4
DETAILED RESULTS ON LSR-SYNTH
We extend the comparison on LSR-Synth to three additional LLM-based equation discovery methods:
LLM-SR (Shojaee et al., 2025a), LaSR (Grayeli et al., 2024), and SGA (Ma et al., 2024a). In addition
to normalized mean squared error (NMSE), we report numeric precision (Acc0.1) and symbolic
accuracy (SA), following the evaluation protocol of LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025b).
For a discovered equation, accuracy to tolerance τ is defined as
Accτ = I

max
1≤i≤Ntest

ˆyi −yi
yi
 ≤τ

,
(16)
where ˆyi and yi denote the predicted and ground-truth values, respectively. We use τ = 0.1 and report
the percentage of problems satisfying this criterion. While NMSE measures aggregate prediction
error, Acc0.1 requires relative error to remain within the specified tolerance at every test point. We
compute both metrics separately on the in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) test sets to
assess interpolation and extrapolation performance.
Symbolic accuracy complements these numerical metrics by assessing whether the discovered
hypothesis recovers the ground-truth symbolic form. Following LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al.,
2025b), we use GPT-4o to judge mathematical equivalence between the predicted and ground-truth
expressions after removing parameters and constants. This model-based assessment accommodates
different representations of equivalent expressions without requiring an exact syntactic match. We
report SA as the percentage of problems judged symbolically equivalent. Unlike the numerical
metrics, SA compares the equations themselves and is therefore reported once per domain, rather
than separately for the ID and OOD splits.
Table 16 summarizes the domain-level results under a common budget of 500 candidate evaluations.
We find that SPECEVO achieves the lowest NMSE in six of the eight domain–split settings, including
three of the four OOD settings. Biology is the exception, where LLM-SR obtains lower NMSE on
both splits. For numeric precision, SPECEVO achieves the highest values on both splits in chemistry,
biology, and physics. In material science, it ties for the highest ID precision, while several baselines
achieve higher OOD precision. The table further shows that SPECEVO achieves the highest SA in
biology (41.66%) and physics (11.36%), while tying for the highest SA in chemistry (13.88%) and
material science (24.0%). These results point to improvements in both numerical prediction and
symbolic-form recovery, and the consistently low OOD NMSE is further evidence of generalization
beyond the training ranges.

paired differences are also positive for every baseline, ranging from +0.87 to +1.64 decades on ID
data and from +0.79 to +1.48 decades on OOD data, with all bootstrap 95% confidence intervals
remaining above zero. The strongest separation is observed against GEPA, for which SPECEVO
wins 109/129 ID problems and 100/129 OOD problems, with mean differences of +1.64 and +1.48
decades, respectively. The aggregate LSR-Synth improvements are thus reflected at the task level:
SPECEVO wins a majority of problems against every baseline under both ID and OOD evaluation.
34


--- Page 35 ---
H
PROMPT TEMPLATES
This appendix reports the prompt templates used by the three functional roles in SPECEVO.
H.1
SPECULATOR
The Speculator uses the lightweight model for high-throughput exploration: it creates initial variants,
reviews archived parents, and applies several mutation and crossover operators. Operator diversity
prevents repeated generic rewrites, while the shared output contract ensures that every accepted
candidate has both executable code and an embeddable strategy description. The six variation
operators share the template below, and Table 18 lists their operator-specific instructions together
with the auxiliary Speculator prompts.
Speculator — Shared template for the six variation operators
You are an expert in optimization heuristics [operator-specific role; see Table 18].
{Task Description}
{Function Signature}
{Parent Program(s) and Score(s):
one parent, or two for crossover}
{Archive Inspirations:
descriptions and scores only}
{Optional Lessons Learned from the Advisor}
{Operator-Specific Instruction:
see Table 18}
{Output Format}
Return exactly three sections in this order: ## Analysis, ## Description, and ## Code. The
analysis must follow the operator-specific structure below. The description must be one plain-prose
paragraph of 2–4 sentences (at most 80 words) naming the algorithmic paradigm, its key data structures, and
its distinguishing mechanism. The code section must contain one fenced python block with the complete,
runnable, self-contained program. The required function signature must match exactly; include every import
and do not use placeholders, ellipses, or incomplete branches.
