H.3
ADVISOR
The Advisor converts deterministic, niche-level search statistics and accumulated failures into short
natural-language guidance.
Advisor — Prompt for population-level reflection
You are a lessons-learned advisor reviewing the search trajectory of an evolutionary code-optimization
system. Write a short prescriptive note that a mutation model will read verbatim before some future attempts.
Do not restate the task or generic constraints already enforced by the evaluator.
{Task Description}
{Function Signature}
{Current State:
best score, evaluations, accept rate, and stagnation}
{Improving Niches:
frontiers advanced in the current window}
{Saturated Niches:
recent attempts, unchanged frontiers, and scores}
{Accumulated Failure Knowledge:
recurrence count and example}
{Previous Advice}
Write exactly the following sections, in this order, using the literal headers and no other Markdown:
WORKING: In 1–2 sentences, name the concrete algorithmic structure or mechanism shared by improving
niches and leaders. Describe the algorithm, not the search process; if nothing is clearly working, say so.
SATURATED: In 1–2 sentences, name the busy strategy families whose frontiers no longer improve and
should be de-emphasized. If there is no clear saturation, write “none.”
AVOID: Provide up to 12 concrete error-prevention instructions as a numbered checklist. Ground each
instruction in the supplied failure evidence or still-applicable previous guidance.
Keep the complete answer under 500 words. Return advice only; do not output code.
I
QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS
This appendix examines one SPECEVO search run on each of two tasks: Circle Packing Rectangle, a
continuous geometric problem, and EPLB, a discrete resource-allocation problem for mixture-of-
experts inference. The evaluation log of each run records every candidate program, the role and
model that produced it, its execution status, and the evaluator message. For each task, we describe
why candidates were rejected, which algorithmic mechanisms the population used, and the guidance
the Advisor derived from the failures. Failure classes are listed from most to least common. We label
how widely each mechanism appears in the population as ubiquitous, common, occasional, or rare; a
program usually combines several mechanisms.
38


--- Page 39 ---
Table 19: Failure classes among rejected candidates on Circle Packing Rectangle, ordered from most
to least common. Each rejected candidate belongs to exactly one class.
Class
What goes wrong
Feasibility
Two circles intersect after the radii are inflated or the layout is rescaled, but the program returns
without rechecking pairwise feasibility
Output shape The returned array does not contain 21 rows with three values each, usually because a helper or
fallback path uses a different representation
Type
Lists and arrays are combined in arithmetic, or a coordinate is missing or infinite
Name
A variable or import is used before being defined, often within a nested helper or early return
branch
Runtime
The program exhausts the evaluation time limit instead of stopping after convergence
Numeric
An array is used directly in a truth test, or a reduction is applied to an empty array
Indexing
An index exceeds the array bounds while circle pairs are enumerated
Syntax
Typographic Unicode symbols or malformed code prevent parsing
I.1
CIRCLE PACKING RECTANGLE
The task is to place 21 non-overlapping circles inside a rectangle of fixed perimeter so as to maximize
the sum of their radii. A configuration that violates feasibility receives no score, even if the violation
is only one part in a thousand.
Recurring errors.
Table 19 lists the failure classes. The most common failure, by a wide margin, is
a pair of overlapping circles. These are not near misses: the overlaps appear when a program inflates
the radii or rescales a finished layout to fill the container and returns it without re-checking pairwise
distances, so relaxing the tolerance would accept almost none of them. The second most common
class is a wrong output shape. The evaluator expects an array with 21 rows, each holding a center and
a radius, but helper functions, early returns, and especially fallback branches, which run only when
the main path fails, often return a different shape. The remaining classes are ordinary programming
faults; a few programs cannot be parsed because they contain typographic Unicode symbols, such as
a minus sign or a less-than-or-equal sign copied from prose.
The same failure classes appear under all model-allocation strategies in Appendix C, and overlapping
circles are the most common failure under every one of them. In those runs, the number of rejections
per quarter of the run stays roughly constant, because no component carries information about earlier
failures forward. In the SPECEVO run, the rejection rate drops substantially from the initialization
phase, which has no Advisor guidance, to the evolutionary phase, in which Advisor notes are included
in Speculator prompts.
The RelayEvolve logs also show how failures differ between the two model tiers. When both models
receive comparable numbers of calls, their rejection rates and overlap rates are similar. Timeouts,
however, come almost entirely from the strong model, whose programs are longer and rely on
expensive global optimizers, whereas indexing and shape errors come mostly from the lightweight
model. SPECEVO uses the lightweight model for high-volume exploration and reserves the strong
model for sparse interventions.
Algorithmic mechanisms.
Table 20 groups the mechanisms by role. Nearly every program starts
from a structured layout, typically hexagonal rows with alternating offsets, and most then search
over the aspect ratio of the rectangle, because its shape determines how many circles fit in each row.
Refinement uses penalty descent on pairwise overlaps, simulated annealing, or damped pairwise
separation. Repair rescales the layout to the perimeter constraint, grows the radii greedily up to the
nearest-neighbor limit, and ends with a shrink pass that removes the remaining overlaps. A wall-clock
guard that returns the best feasible configuration found so far is present in almost every program.
The initialization phase and the Speculators introduce individual mechanisms and refine them one at
a time, so the record improves in small steps. In this run, the Navigator’s record-setting interventions
combined existing mechanisms instead of introducing new ones. The final best program initializes a
hexagonal layout, relaxes it with damped pairwise separation, grows the radii toward their nearest-
neighbor limits, adds a backtracking enlargement pass for each circle, rescales to the perimeter

Advisor feedback.
The box below shows the guidance the Advisor had consolidated by the end of
the run. Each item is an instruction for one failure class, not a diagnosis of a single program, and the
items are ordered by the number of rejected candidates they address. The note is rewritten at every
checkpoint instead of extended, which keeps it short enough to include verbatim, and it is added
to only a fraction of Speculator prompts so that it does not push the whole population toward one
defensive coding style.
Consolidated Advisor guidance: Circle Packing Rectangle
1. Ensure that no two circles overlap by keeping the distance between their centers at least equal to
the sum of their radii minus the tolerance, as the validator requires.
2. Return exactly 21 circles as an array with 21 rows and three values per row, and preserve this
shape through every operation.
3. Convert all coordinates and radii to double precision before arithmetic, and ensure that no value
is missing or infinite.
4. Define and import every name before use, and call only documented public interfaces.
5. Keep the total runtime below the evaluation limit by bounding iteration counts and stopping early
after convergence.
6. Confirm that an array is nonempty before using it in a truth test or a reduction.
7. Clip indices to the actual array size, especially when enumerating circle pairs.

with their ASCII equivalents.
9. Clip radii to a small positive lower bound before any geometric computation to avoid division by
zero and invalid square roots.
I.2
EPLB
The task is to place logical experts onto physical GPU slots for mixture-of-experts inference. Given
load statistics for each layer, a program decides how many replicas each expert receives and which
slot each replica occupies, subject to a fixed replica budget, a fixed hierarchy of groups, nodes, and
GPUs, and a capacity limit for each GPU. The problem is discrete, and a program must keep three
indices consistent as replica counts change: the logical expert, the replica, and the physical slot.
Recurring errors.
Table 21 lists the failure classes. On Circle Packing Rectangle, most rejected
programs violate a geometric constraint; on EPLB, indexing errors dominate: a slot or replica index
computed from capacity arithmetic exceeds the bounds of the tensor it indexes, even when the
allocation policy itself is sound. Two classes have a single main cause. Most name errors come from
programs that schedule each replica on the least-loaded GPU with a priority queue, implement the
queue operations correctly, and never import the priority-queue module; some of these programs also
call heap routines of the tensor library that do not exist. Most type errors come from a deterministic
hash initialization, which multiplies a large hexadecimal constant by a slot index to spread the replicas
of an expert across devices without a random number generator. Unless the product is reduced modulo
the number of GPUs before it is used as an index, it overflows the integer range and yields an index
far outside the tensor. Nearly every overflow rejection in the run came from a program containing
such a constant, and a single guidance item can remove this defect while keeping the mechanism.
The rejection rate decreases throughout the run, with the largest drop between the initialization
phase and the evolutionary phase. The mechanical faults that are frequent early on, namely the
missing import, the overflowing constant, and the invalid slot index, are among the failure signatures
accumulated by the Advisor. They are largely absent from the later population, although the same
algorithmic ideas remain in use.
Algorithmic mechanisms.
Table 22 lists the mechanisms. The interface imposes a per-layer
solution and the group, node, and GPU hierarchy, so programs differ in three decisions. To choose
the number of replicas per expert, most programs repeatedly give the next replica to the expert whose
load per replica it reduces most, which is the classical apportionment rule (some programs implement
it explicitly as Huntington–Hill); a substantial minority instead binary-search a load threshold and
give each expert enough replicas to fall below it, and the strongest programs use the threshold search
to approach the budget and the marginal-gain rule to correct the remainder. To assign slots, programs
use a modular or rotated round-robin walk over the GPUs, which spreads the replicas of each expert

across devices, or a priority queue that places each replica on the least-loaded GPU. To enforce
feasibility, most programs clamp to capacity, fill the remaining slots in a repair pass, and assert that
the replica counts sum to the budget; the Advisor reinforces these mechanisms.
As on Circle Packing Rectangle, the Navigator’s SYNTHESIS and SURGICAL interventions produce
strong, valid programs that reinforce the incumbent design. Its later REFRAME interventions, which
introduce a strategy family absent from the population, score below the incumbent. This is expected:
REFRAME is triggered by stagnation to increase diversity, and the archive keeps these programs as
parents even when they do not improve the record. The final record was set by a lightweight structural
crossover that combines threshold-based replica allocation with the marginal-gain correction and
a placement that respects the hierarchical capacity constraints; its structure came from an earlier
Navigator proposal that lightweight variants then refined.
Advisor feedback.
The EPLB guidance below is more mechanical than the Circle Packing Rect-
angle guidance, because most rejected EPLB programs use sound allocation policies and fail on
indexing, imports, or element types.
Consolidated Advisor guidance: EPLB
1. Clip every index to the valid range of the dimension it addresses, keeping physical and logical
indices within bounds and consistent with the expected shapes.
2. Import all required modules, including the priority queue module, at the top of the program, and
call only documented public interfaces rather than private tensor library routines.
3. Convert tensor values to the intended element type before use, and maintain that type consistently
across operations.
4. Ensure that replica counts sum to the replica budget for every layer, and clamp them to both the
budget and the available GPU capacity.
5. Bound the number of placement iterations so that the program remains within the evaluation time
limit.
42


--- Page 43 ---
6. Give the mapping from logical to physical indices the required three dimensions, with the final
extent equal to the largest replica count.
7. Pass tensor shapes as tuples of integers rather than as a single integer.
8. Reduce a tensor to a scalar before using it in a truth test.
9. Return exactly the three required tensors in the order specified by the function signature.
10. Use only plain ASCII characters because a typographic hyphen is not valid syntax.
11. Use floor rounding rather than ceiling rounding in integer division so that the result matches the
expected element type.
In both tasks, a few instructions cover most of the observed failures, and the first instructions concern
output and feasibility requirements, not the algorithm. A stronger model alone would not be expected
to remove these failures: in the RelayEvolve runs, the strong and lightweight models fail at similar
overall rates and differ mainly in which requirements they violate. The difference in SPECEVO is that
this evidence is carried forward: the note is rebuilt at every checkpoint from all accumulated failure
signatures, so a failure observed early in the run still affects later proposals.
43
